props.title: How I Won the War
props.initialSlug: Lennon stars in surreal WWII dark comedy satire

sections.content: How I Won the War (1967) stands as Richard Lester's boldest anti-war statement, arriving at the height of Vietnam War protests. The film stars John Lennon in his only non-Beatles acting role, marking a fascinating intersection between counterculture music and experimental cinema. Lester's approach deliberately shatters war film conventions established by films like The Bridge on the River Kwai (1957), using surreal comedy and fourth-wall breaks to emphasize war's absurdity. The film's influence echoes in later satirical war films like MASH (1970) and Catch-22 (1970).

sections.content: Lester's experimental techniques in How I Won the War fundamentally challenged traditional war film narratives. His use of color-tinted stock footage, direct address to camera, and non-linear storytelling influenced later works like Full Metal Jacket (1987) and Three Kings (1999). The film's portrayal of Lieutenant Goodbody (Michael Crawford) as an incompetent officer continues to resonate with anti-authoritarian war films like Buffalo Soldiers (2001). SUBHEAD: Impact on Counter-Culture Cinema

The film's release coincided with John Lennon's increasing political activism, making it a crucial document of 1960s counterculture cinema. Its influence extends beyond war films into the broader experimental narrative tradition, connecting to works like Performance (1970) and If.... (1968). Lester's techniques from The Running Jumping & Standing Still Film (1959) evolved here into a sophisticated critique of military mythology.
